content: Obesity is a well-established risk factor for several cancers, including breast, colorectal, and gynecologic malignancies¹⁻². Emerging evidence indicates that obesity not only contributes to cancer development but also significantly influences clinical outcomes. For instance, higher body mass index (BMI) is associated with poorer prognosis in patients with breast³⁻⁴ and colorectal⁵⁻⁶ cancers. In contrast, some studies report paradoxical associations—namely, improved survival in obese patients diagnosed with gastric⁷ or renal⁸ cancer—a phenomenon sometimes referred to as the “obesity paradox.” These divergent findings underscore the complexity of obesity–cancer interactions and highlight the need for cancer-type–specific investigations into underlying biological mechanisms.
